title: Transfer: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
oneLiner: Change at most k letters to get the longest run of one letter. Same variable window as the no-repeats lesson; only the rule it keeps changes.
keyTakeaway: A window can become all one letter with at most k changes exactly when its length minus the count of its most common letter is at most k. Keep letter counts for the window, grow right every step, and shrink from the left while length - maxCount > k. Each index enters and leaves once: O(n).
explanation:
This follows Longest Substring Without Repeats with the rule changed. You get a string s of uppercase letters and a number k. You may change any character to any other uppercase letter, at most k times in total. Return the length of the longest run of one repeated letter you can end up with. For "AABABBA" and k = 1 the answer is 4: change the middle A of "BABB" to get "BBBB".

Look at one window and ask what it costs to make it all one letter. The cheapest plan keeps the letter that already appears most often and changes everything else, so the cost is the window length minus the count of its most common letter. The window is usable when that cost is at most k. That is the rule the window has to keep, in place of "no character twice".

The loop is the one you already know. Keep a count per letter (an array of 26) for the window. Move right forward, add s[right] to the counts and update maxCount, the largest count seen. While (right - left + 1) - maxCount > k, the window costs too much: subtract s[left] from the counts and move left forward. Then record right - left + 1 if it is the best so far.

A detail that surprises people: when you shrink, you do not need to lower maxCount. A stale, too high maxCount can only let a window that is not truly valid survive at the same length as the best one already found, never longer, so the answer is unchanged. The answer only grows when a real letter count beats the old maxCount. Recomputing the true maximum over 26 counts is also fine; it is O(26) per step, still O(n) overall.

The visualization runs "AABABBA" with k = 1; the highlighted cells are the window.

Explain why the same idea works: before you move on, write two or three sentences comparing this with Longest Substring Without Repeats. What is the rule each window keeps, why is it still safe to shrink only from the left when the rule breaks, and why does the scan stay O(n)?

recognitionSignals: Longest contiguous run you can make uniform (or valid) with a budget of at most k changes, flips or deletions.
Whether a window is fixable depends only on counts inside it, so adding on the right and removing on the left are cheap.
gotchas: The cost of a window is its length minus the count of its MOST common letter, not the number of distinct letters.
Shrink while the cost is above k (a while loop, as in the parent lesson), and only then measure the window.
k can be larger than the string: the answer is then the whole length, not more.
confusableWith: Sliding Window (Variable Size): Longest Substring Without Repeats keeps "no character twice"; this keeps "at most k characters differ from the most common one". Same loop, different rule.

complexity.note: right visits each index once and left only moves forward, so each character enters and leaves the window at most once. The counts are one per letter of a fixed 26 letter alphabet; recomputing their maximum each step is O(26), still constant.

referenceSolutions.python:
def character_replacement(s, k):
    counts = {}
    left = 0
    max_count = 0
    best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) + 1
        max_count = max(max_count, counts[ch])
        # Too many letters differ from the most common one: shrink from the left.
        while (right - left + 1) - max_count > k:
            counts[s[left]] -= 1
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
